title: [Bug] silent imap death

judge.reasoning:
Both patches target the same failure mode: node-imap can emit `error` without a following `close`, and the existing `onTransportError` only called `lose()` and returned when a restore was possible, waiting on a close that never comes. That leaves exactly the symptom the issue describes: no 'closed unexpectedly' log (it is tied to `close`), no reconnect, no error handler, and a SELECT that hangs forever if the error lands mid-dial.

Patch B fixes that root cause directly and narrowly: `onTransportError` now starts `restore()` itself (and reports when restoring is impossible), the dialling transport's error is let go through the SELECT rather than tearing down the installed one, and `selectMailbox` rejects on `error` so a reconnect attempt cannot hang. Its tests exercise precisely the issue scenario (error with no close → reconnect; tries exhausted → `close('dropped')` reaches the caller; fresh transport erroring under SELECT is released) and would fail on the old code. Changes are ~40 lines in one file with no behaviour change for users.

Patch A replaces the IMAP library wholesale (node-imap → imapflow), adds a vendored patch to imapflow, rewrites header parsing, attachment handling, part selection, and introduces a new search-criteria translator that now throws on activation for inputs previously accepted (empty criteria, `KEYWORD \Recent`, colliding keys handled via De Morgan rewrites), changes `addFlags`' signature, drops rfc2047 filename decoding in favour of driver metadata, and rewrites essentially every test in the package. Its genuine strength is liveness detection via `maxIdleTime`/`socketTimeout`, verified against a fake server that goes silent, which would also catch a truly wedged socket. But that advantage is bought with a multi-thousand-line redesign whose correctness cannot be established from the diff, that buries the actual fix, and that carries real regression risk for existing workflows (stricter criteria compilation, output/attachment naming differences, a patched dependency). Under the stated weighting, that extra scope counts against A because it adds risk and obscures the fix.

The independent tests crashed on all three trees, so they provide no signal. On the evidence in front of me, B resolves the identified root cause with targeted, meaningful tests and minimal risk; A's broader detection does not outweigh the risk and opacity of a full library migration as the fix for this bug.

### Bug Description

The Email Trigger (IMAP) node can silently lose its connection without producing any log output, without triggering a reconnection attempt, and without invoking the configured Error Handler workflow. The workflow continues to show as "Published" (active) in the UI, but the IMAP trigger is effectively dead. Incoming emails remain unprocessed indefinitely. The user has no way to detect this condition other than manually noticing unread emails.

### Additional context
This was observed after a Hetzner Cloud Firewall rule change that temporarily interrupted connectivity on port 993. Under normal circumstances, IMAP disconnects are logged and trigger reconnection attempts. In this case, the connection was lost during or after the firewall change, and the trigger node entered a state where it believed it was still connected but had no active TCP socket.
The forceReconnect option (set to 55 minutes) did not recover the connection either, suggesting the internal reconnect timer may also have died silently.
Related: #29996 (Options-only changes not restarting triggers on Publish)

### To Reproduce

The exact trigger for the silent failure is not yet identified, but the following sequence was observed:

1. Workflow "Parse DMARC reports…" is active with an Email Trigger (IMAP) node (typeVersion 2) and forceReconnect: 55 configured
2. The IMAP trigger is connected and processing emails normally
3. An external event disrupts the IMAP connection (in this case: a Hetzner Cloud Firewall rule for port 993 was temporarily removed and re-added)
4. The IMAP trigger loses its connection
5. No Email Read Imap: Connected closed unexpectedly log message is produced
6. No reconnection attempt is logged
7. No Error Handler workflow is triggered
8. The workflow continues to show "Published" in the UI
9. ss -tn | grep 993 inside the container confirms: no active TCP connection to the IMAP server
10. Emails accumulate unread in the mailbox
11. Only a full container restart (docker restart) re-establishes the IMAP connection

### Expected behavior

When an IMAP connection is lost, the trigger node should:

1. Log the disconnection event (as it normally does with "Connected closed unexpectedly")
2. Attempt to reconnect (with exponential backoff, as it normally does)
3. If reconnection fails permanently, invoke the configured Error Handler workflow
4. The workflow status in the UI should reflect the actual state of the trigger

A silently dead trigger with no logging, no reconnection, and no error notification is the worst possible failure mode — the user has no indication that mail processing has stopped.

title: Javascript expression: Using ` (template literals) adds UNINTENDED SPACE after underscore if there's a fixed string before it

judge.reasoning:
Both patches apply the same root-cause fix: they stop replacing individual TemplateElements (which recast patches in place, inserting a space between a trailing identifier character like `_` and the following `${`) and instead rebuild the whole TemplateLiteral with `original = null` so recast reprints it from scratch. Both gate the rebuild on the literal containing a real newline, so literals without newlines are no longer touched at all. On the core issue they are equivalent and both resolve the `chk_ 123` symptom at its cause.

The differentiator is a side effect of reprinting the whole literal. Recast's printer builds each quasi via `fromString(raw)`, which treats leading whitespace as indentation and re-emits leading tabs as spaces when concatenating. In the base code only quasis containing a newline were reprinted; with the whole-literal rebuild, every quasi of a multiline literal is reprinted, so a quasi such as `\tb_` that previously survived untouched now has its leading tab expanded to spaces under Patch A. Patch B anticipates this by escaping tabs to `\t` in the rebuilt elements (a semantically identical change to the cooked value, consistent with how newlines are already escaped) and adds a 'keeps tabs' test for it. This is adjacent to the issue, but it directly neutralises a regression the shared approach would otherwise widen, so it counts as a correctness advantage rather than scope creep.

Tests: Patch B's suite is more thorough and more faithful to the report: a direct `people.map(p => \`...\`).join('')` reproduction, fixed text plus multiple code chunks, nested literals, tagged templates, tabs, and a workflow-package test with the issue's expression shape. Patch A adds two tournament tests plus a compatibility-corpus row that cover the core case and nesting but less of the surrounding surface. All of these tests would fail on base and pass after their respective patch for the core scenario; neither could be executed by the harness (all runs crashed), so I weighed them on content only.

Craft is comparable: A uses an object spread with an `original: null` type intersection, B assigns `literal.original = null` on a `{ original?: null }` type; both are clear, and B's comment explains the recast behaviour in more detail. Overall B is the better fix by a modest but real margin on correctness at the edges and on test coverage.

title: Email Trigger IMAP broken

judge.reasoning:
The issue describes a trigger that silently stops firing: no error, no execution, mail left unread, and arrivals never processed again. In the base code arrival handlers are serialised, so any handler that never settles silences the connection for good. Patch B identifies a concrete way that happens with node-imap: a UID FETCH for a message expunged or moved between SEARCH and FETCH simply ends with fewer messages than asked for, and both `search` and `getPartData` wait on the missing message forever. B makes `search` resolve on fetch `end` (deferred one macrotask so in-flight message parsing finishes first) and makes `getPartData` reject with a new `MessagePartMissingError`, so a vanished message either yields a shorter batch or surfaces as a reported handler error rather than a permanent hang. It also wraps `getMessage` failures so an unknown encoding rejects instead of leaving an unhandled rejection. This is a minimal, root-cause-directed change in the exact code path the issue implicates, consistent with a regression story around the serialised queue, and it ships a dedicated test file (omitted for size, ~6 KB) for the package. The independent tests were written around the same vanished-message scenario, though they crashed on every tree so they add no evidence either way.

Patch A replaces node-imap with imapflow across the whole `@n8n/imap` package and both node versions, adds a vendored patch to imapflow's IDLE handling, reimplements search-criteria translation with its own semantics (empty criteria now throw, dates are reformatted, colliding keys are De Morgan-wrapped, several imapflow quirks are documented as undetectable), removes the charset/transfer-encoding decoders, changes error types, and alters activation behaviour (`catchUp` on start). It would also resolve the hung-fetch scenario, since imapflow's fetch generator ends on the tagged response regardless of message count, and it adds liveness detection for a wedged socket, which is its stated hypothesis for the issue. But that hypothesis is an assumption the issue does not establish, and the fix is a driver migration whose surface area dwarfs the reported problem. For a production regression this is the kind of broader redesign the scope criterion says to count against a patch when it adds risk: a dependency swap plus a hand-patched upstream, new search-compilation edge cases, and behaviour changes that could break existing workflows cannot be validated from the diff alone, and the extensive new tests mostly exercise the new design rather than demonstrate the reported failure. A's tests are thorough, but tests for a rewrite do not offset the risk the rewrite introduces.

On correctness both plausibly fix the issue, with A covering an additional hypothesis at very high cost; on scope and risk B is clearly better; on craft both are clean, but A's imapflow patch is a maintenance liability. B is the better fix for this issue.

### Bug Description

Two independent bugs in the ERPNext node's Document → Get Many operation with "Return All" enabled:

**1. Duplicates one row per page boundary once a doctype has more than 1000 records.**

The pagination loop advances `limit_start` by `limit_page_length - 1` instead of `limit_page_length`:

https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/98f69ed52cca22b118b68ef88c7f2152c539d218/packages/nodes-base/nodes/ERPNext/GenericFunctions.ts#L79-L86

With the default page size of 1000, page 2 starts at `limit_start = 999` instead of `1000`, so it re-fetches record 999 — the last record of page 1 — as its own first record of page 2. This repeats at every page boundary. It's invisible on any doctype with fewer than 1000 rows, which is likely why it's gone unnoticed.

**2. Touching the Options block without adding a filter throws before any request is made.**

https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/98f69ed52cca22b118b68ef88c7f2152c539d218/packages/nodes-base/nodes/ERPNext/ERPNext.node.ts#L178-L184

The Filters fixedCollection's own field definition defaults to `{}`, not `{ customProperty: [] }`:

https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/98f69ed52cca22b118b68ef88c7f2152c539d218/packages/nodes-base/nodes/ERPNext/DocumentDescription.ts#L128-L133

`{}` is truthy, so `if (filters)` passes, and `filters.customProperty` is `undefined` on that default shape — `.map()` throws a `TypeError` before any HTTP request happens. This is exactly what the `// TODO: filters not working` comment sitting directly above the code is flagging.

Both are separate from #19271 (double URL-encoding a doctype name with spaces, already claimed by #22338) and from #35796 / #17267 (System Manager role requirement on the Fields/Filters dropdowns) — this issue is only about the two bugs above.

### To Reproduce

**Bug 1:** Add an ERPNext node, Document → Get Many, pick a DocType with more than 1000 records, enable Return All, execute. The result contains one duplicate record per 1000-record boundary crossed.

**Bug 2:** Add an ERPNext node, Document → Get Many, pick any DocType, open **Options** and add a **Field** (or otherwise cause the Options collection to be touched) without adding anything under **Filters**, execute.

### Expected behavior

Bug 1: Return All returns exactly one row per record, no duplicates.
Bug 2: The node should not throw when Filters is left empty; the request should proceed without a `filters` query parameter.

### Actual behavior

Bug 1: one duplicate row per page boundary.
Bug 2: unhandled `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')` (or similar, depending on engine) before any request is sent.

### Bug Description

When using the **Home Assistant** node with resource **State** and operation **Upsert**, the node always includes an empty `attributes: {}` object in the request body when no State Attributes are configured. The Home Assistant `POST /api/states/<entity_id>` endpoint replaces an entity's attributes with whatever is sent, so upserting only a state (without attributes) **wipes any existing attributes** on that entity.

Root cause: in `packages/nodes-base/nodes/HomeAssistant/HomeAssistant.node.ts`, the upsert body is built as `{ state, attributes: {} }` and the empty `attributes` object is sent unconditionally.

Secondary issue found in the same code path: because the attributes object was initialized but then written via a computed key on a body that no longer had the key after a partial fix, setting attributes could also throw
`Cannot set properties of undefined`. The fix only sends `attributes` when the user actually provides them.

### To Reproduce

1. In Home Assistant, create/pick an entity that has attributes (e.g. a `sensor` with `unit_of_measurement` and `friendly_name`).
2. In n8n, add a **Home Assistant** node → Resource: **State** → Operation: **Upsert**.
3. Set the **Entity ID** and a new **State**, and leave **State Attributes** empty.
4. Execute the node.
5. Check the entity in Home Assistant → its previously set attributes have been removed (only the new state remains).

### Expected behavior

Upserting a state without configuring any State Attributes should update only the state and leave the entity's existing attributes untouched - i.e. the request body should not include an `attributes` property when none are provided. Attributes should only be sent when the user explicitly sets them.

## Bug Description

`packages/cli/src/crash-journal.ts` resolves the journal to `join(n8nFolder, 'crash.journal')` with no way to override that path. In a multi-main deployment where the `main` instances share one `N8N_USER_FOLDER` on a shared writable volume, every process resolves to the same file, and both halves of the mechanism then interfere with each other:

- `init()` logs `Last session crashed` at **error** level and `sleep(10_000)` whenever the file already exists at start-up. The second `main` to start always finds the journal the first one has just touched, so it reports a crash that never happened and delays its own start by 10 seconds.
- `cleanup()` unlinks the journal on graceful shutdown. When one `main` is replaced during a rolling deployment, its shutdown deletes the journal belonging to the process that is *still running* — so after a deployment no running `main` has a journal at all, and a genuine crash is not reported on the next start.

n8n already solved this exact class of problem for the event-bus log by adding `N8N_EVENTBUS_LOGWRITER_LOGFULLPATH`, whose documentation states that processes sharing one writable volume must each be given a unique absolute path and that the orchestrator owns that uniqueness. The crash journal has no equivalent knob.

## To Reproduce

1. Run two `main` instances sharing one `N8N_USER_FOLDER` on a shared writable volume (here: an NFS access point mounted at `/home/node/.n8n`, queue mode, `NODE_ENV=production` from the official image so `inProduction` is true).
2. Start them a few seconds apart, as a rolling deployment does.
3. The **later** of the two logs `{"level":"error","message":"Last session crashed","metadata":{"file":"crash-journal.js","function":"init"}}` even though neither process crashed, and pauses for 10 seconds before continuing.
4. Now let a rolling deployment replace both. Once the outgoing processes have exited gracefully, run `find / -name crash.journal` from a container mounting the same volume: it returns nothing, while both new `main` processes are running normally.

## Expected behavior

Each n8n process should have its own crash journal, so that `Last session crashed` reflects that process having actually crashed, and so that one process's shutdown cannot delete another's journal. Either of these would be enough:

- an env override for the journal path (e.g. `N8N_CRASH_JOURNAL_PATH`), mirroring `N8N_EVENTBUS_LOGWRITER_LOGFULLPATH`; or
- deriving the filename per instance. Note the event-bus log's process-type suffix would not be sufficient on its own here, since these processes are all of type `main` — it would need a host or instance id.

A per-process `N8N_USER_FOLDER` is the only workaround available today, and it is unattractive because that folder also holds source-control state, community nodes and the filesystem binary-data store, none of which anyone wants to relocate to fix a log line.

## Debug Info

Observed across three consecutive rolling deployments of a two-`main` deployment. In each one, the second process to start logged the message and the first did not:

| deployment | first process starts | second process starts | logs `Last session crashed` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 13:52:00Z | 13:52:30Z | second, at 13:53:32Z |
| 2 | 14:10:48Z | 14:11:09Z | second, at 14:12:22Z |
| 3 | 14:46:21Z | 14:46:52Z | second, at 14:47:45Z |

Relevant call sites: `base-command.ts` wires `CrashJournal.init()` via `initCrashJournal()` and `CrashJournal.cleanup()` via `exitSuccessFully()`; `start.ts` and `worker.ts` both call `initCrashJournal()`. Workers are unaffected in our setup because they do not mount the shared volume, so each has a private journal.

To be clear about impact: nothing is lost. The journal is read by nothing other than `init()`, and execution recovery is handled by the event bus, not by this file. The cost is a false error-level log line on every deployment — which is misleading during incident triage and pollutes error dashboards — plus 10 seconds of avoidable start-up delay on one process.

## Operating System

Alpine Linux 3.24 (official n8n Docker image), on AWS ECS Fargate

## n8n Version

2.36.9

## Node.js Version

24.18.1

## Database

PostgreSQL

## Execution mode

queue

issue_md:
### Bug Description

When the AI Agent (Tools Agent) V3 node has `retryOnFail: true` and hits its own `maxIterations` limit, the generic node-level retry mechanism retries the node's `execute()` without understanding the Agent's suspend/resume (`EngineRequest`/`EngineResponse`) protocol. This silently wipes all accumulated tool-call history and restarts the task from scratch, instead of surfacing a clean "max iterations reached" error. Critically, this can repeat indefinitely (not just once) - see mechanism below - resulting in unbounded, costly LLM/tool-call loops with no natural stopping point.

**Root cause (traced in source)**

- `checkMaxIterations()` (`packages/@n8n/nodes-langchain/.../ToolsAgent/V3/helpers/checkMaxIterations.ts`) throws a `NodeOperationError` once `response.metadata.iterationCount >= maxIterations`.
- This is caught by the engine's generic retry loop in `packages/core/src/execution-engine/workflow-execute.ts`, which retries `runNode()` per `retryOnFail`/`maxTries`/`waitBetweenTries` - with no awareness of the Agent's own suspend/resume protocol.
- On retry, `toolsAgentExecute` is re-invoked and empirically receives no prior tool-call history, rather than continuing where it left off.
- The retry budget (`maxTries`) is scoped to a single "dequeue" of the node from the execution stack (one resume attempt), NOT the whole execution. Since a "successful" (even if context-reset) round returns a fresh `EngineRequest` and triggers `continue executionLoop` in the outer loop, the retry counter is effectively reset every `maxIterations` rounds. The reset-and-restart pattern is therefore NOT bounded by `maxTries` and can repeat for as many cycles as the task allows.

**Empirical evidence**

- The LLM prompt byte-length reverts to the exact baseline size (identical to the very first call) at every reset point - confirmed across 11 consecutive reset-cycles in one execution (105 total tool calls for a task that should have needed far fewer).
- A clean timing signature: the gap between a reset boundary's last tool-call completion and the next LLM call's start is consistently ~2000ms longer than normal round-to-round gaps (~500ms) - matching `waitBetweenTries: 2000` exactly, reproduced across multiple independent occurrences.
- Confirmed causally: disabling `retryOnFail` on the same node/task eliminates the reset entirely - the workflow now fails cleanly with "Max iterations (N) reached..." instead of resetting.

**Suggested fix**

`retryOnFail` should either not apply to a `NodeOperationError` thrown from `checkMaxIterations` (a deterministic, non-transient limit - not a transient failure retry could plausibly help with), or, when retrying an Agent V3 node mid-suspend/resume, the retry should preserve/reconstruct the full prior context before re-invoking `execute()`, so it genuinely continues instead of silently restarting.

**Current workaround**

Disable `retryOnFail` entirely on Agent V3 nodes. The node then fails cleanly (routable via `onError: continueErrorOutput`) instead of retrying - no functionality is lost, since retryOnFail's only observed effect here is the harmful reset behavior.

**Possibly related**

### Bug Description

AI Agent V3 can reconstruct tool-call history with a node-derived tool name instead of the canonical LangChain tool name that was originally selected by the model.

On current `master` (`f7f92c7107e72f8151392b7fdf22bdf660df6892`), `createEngineRequests()` already stores the canonical tool name in `action.metadata.toolName`, but `buildSteps.resolveToolName()` does not read that field. For standalone tools it can fall back to `nodeNameToToolName(action.nodeName)` instead.

If the node display name and the registered tool name differ — for example after a node rename/paste suffix or when a Tool Workflow uses a custom tool name — the reconstructed history can therefore expose a different tool name to the model. If the model reuses that reconstructed name on the next turn, `createEngineRequests()` cannot find it in the canonical tool list and silently filters the action out. The agent can then continue with no tool observation and eventually hit max iterations.

I reproduced this deterministically on current `master` without model/network nondeterminism.

### To Reproduce

A focused source-level reproduction is enough:

1. Register a standalone tool whose canonical LangChain name is `Ingredient_Glossary_Lookup`.
2. Give its source node the display name `Ingredient Glossary Lookup1`.
3. Let `createEngineRequests()` create an engine action. The action correctly contains:
   `metadata.toolName = "Ingredient_Glossary_Lookup"`.
4. Pass that action through `buildSteps()`.
5. Current behavior reconstructs `steps[].action.tool` as `Ingredient_Glossary_Lookup1` instead of the canonical name.
6. Feed that reconstructed name into `createEngineRequests()` with only `Ingredient_Glossary_Lookup` registered.
7. The result is an empty action list because the tool lookup fails and the item is filtered out.

Fail-before proof:
- canonical-name reconstruction test: fails
- round-trip executable-action test: fails
- matching-name control: passes
- HITL precedence control: passes
- toolkit `input.tool` precedence control: passes
- silent-drop behavior control: passes

A narrow local fix — reading `action.metadata.toolName` before falling back to `nodeNameToToolName(action.nodeName)` — makes all 6 proof cases pass while preserving HITL/toolkit precedence. The existing neighboring `buildSteps` + `createEngineRequests` suites also pass: 74/74, for 80/80 total.

### Expected behavior

When reconstructing Agent V3 tool-call history, n8n should preserve the canonical LangChain tool name that `createEngineRequests()` already stores in `action.metadata.toolName`.

The node display name should only be a final fallback when no canonical tool identity is available.

### Debug Info

Source-level deterministic proof on:

- repository: `n8n-io/n8n`
- branch: `master`
- commit: `f7f92c7107e72f8151392b7fdf22bdf660df6892`
- affected area:
  - `packages/@n8n/nodes-langchain/utils/agent-execution/createEngineRequests.ts`
  - `packages/@n8n/nodes-langchain/utils/agent-execution/buildSteps.ts`
  - `packages/@n8n/nodes-langchain/utils/agent-execution/types.ts`
- validation:
  - fail-before causal reproduction
  - 6/6 focused proof tests after the narrow fix
  - 74/74 neighboring repository tests
  - `git diff --check` clean

`RequestResponseMetadata.toolName` is already documented as the LangChain tool name preserved for reverse lookup, so the minimal fix appears to align with the existing design rather than introduce a new behavior.

Related but not duplicates:
- #37916: V1 schema-invalid tool calls; the V3 tool-name drift was only noted later in comments.
- #36883: V3 silent tool-call drops with a different reported trigger/mechanism.

If the team agrees this is a separate V3 bug and this scope is acceptable for a community contribution, I can send the narrow fix with regression coverage.

### Environment

This report uses a deterministic source-level reproduction against current `master`; it does not depend on a specific hosted deployment, database, execution mode, or external model provider.

Scope and craft: A's change is larger (signature change, four call sites per version, error-handler tweak) but all of it is in service of the fix and is coherent and well-commented. ## Describe the bug

`Splunk` node, `Search Job > Create`: `earliest_time` / `latest_time` / `index_earliest` / `index_latest` are passed through `toUnixEpoch()`, which is:

```js
function toUnixEpoch(timestamp) {
    return Date.parse(timestamp) / 1000;
}
```

`Date.parse` returns `NaN` for every Splunk relative time specifier (`-15m`, `-24h`, `-1d@d`, `now`, `@d`). `NaN / 1000` is `NaN`, and `NaN` is then sent to Splunk as the literal string `NaN`.

**Splunk accepts `earliest_time=NaN` with HTTP 201 and silently ignores the bound.** So the search runs over a different — much wider — time range than the user asked for, with no error anywhere.

**Measured** against Splunk 10.2.1, `search index=_internal | stats count`:

| `earliest_time` sent | events returned |
|---|---|
| `-5m` (what the user typed) | 1,462 |
| `NaN` (what the node actually sends) | 12,027 |
| omitted entirely (all time) | 12,029 |

The node returns ~8× the requested data and reports success. For alerting, metrics or any rate-based logic this is silent data corruption rather than a visible failure.

Splunk's own API accepts relative specifiers directly — no conversion is needed:

| `earliest_time` | HTTP |
|---|---|
| `-1d@d` | 201 |
| `-15m` | 201 |
| `-24h` | 201 |

## Prior report

This was reported as #10447 (Aug 2024) and closed `NOT_PLANNED` as "working as expected… we don't currently support the relative time options". Respectfully, the measurement above shows the outcome is not merely an unsupported input: an unsupported input that is silently converted to `NaN` and then silently ignored by the server produces **wrong results that look correct**. Rejecting the input with a clear error would be "not supported"; this is not that.

## To Reproduce

1. Splunk node, Resource `Search Job`, Operation `Create`.
2. Search: `search index=_internal | stats count`
3. Additional Fields: `Earliest Time` = `-5m`, `Latest Time` = `now`.
4. Execute, then fetch the job's results.
5. Compare with the same search issued directly to `/services/search/jobs` with `earliest_time=-5m`.

The node's count matches an all-time search, not a 5-minute one.

## Expected behavior

Pass relative specifiers through unchanged (Splunk parses them natively), and apply `toUnixEpoch` only to absolute timestamps — or validate and reject an unparseable value with an explicit error instead of emitting `NaN`. Under no circumstance should an unparseable time bound become a silently wider search.

## Operating System

Docker (n8nio/n8n), macOS host

## n8n Version

2.38.7

## Node.js Version

24.x (container default)

## Database

SQLite

## Execution mode

### Bug Description

n8n Agents (the first-class `agents` module) configured with the **MiniMax** provider (`minimax/MiniMax-M3`, credential type `minimaxApi`) fail with

```
The model reached its output token limit before it returned an answer. Reduce the request scope or use another model.
```

whenever a single model turn needs more than **4096 output tokens** (long final answer, or reasoning + answer). The same agent, same prompt and same model through OpenRouter (`openrouter/minimax/minimax-m3`) completes normally, because that path does not send `max_tokens`.

Root cause (traced in the installed code):

1. `@n8n/agents/dist/runtime/model/model-factory.js` builds the `minimax` provider with `@ai-sdk/minimax`, which wraps `AnthropicLanguageModel` and talks to MiniMax's **Anthropic-compatible** endpoint (`https://api.minimax.io/anthropic/v1`). The Anthropic Messages API requires `max_tokens` on every request.
2. `@n8n/agents/dist/runtime/model/provider-quirks.js` only sets a default output limit for Kimi:
   ```js
   function resolveDefaultMaxOutputTokens(modelId) {
       if (modelId.toLowerCase().includes('kimi-k3')) {
           return exports.HIGH_REASONING_DEFAULT_MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS; // 65_536
       }
       return undefined;
   }
   ```
3. With `maxOutputTokens` undefined, `@ai-sdk/anthropic` (`getModelCapabilities`) treats `MiniMax-M3` as an unknown model and falls back to `maxOutputTokens: 4096`, so every request is sent with `max_tokens: 4096` (plus a `compatibility` warning that is not surfaced to the user).
4. There is no way to override it: the Agent JSON `config` schema (`reasoning`, `promptCaching`, `webSearch`, `toolCallConcurrency`, `maxIterations`) does not accept `maxOutputTokens`, and the runtime only passes `execOptions.maxOutputTokens` internally.

MiniMax-M3 supports up to 512k output tokens, so 4096 is far below the model's capability and below what a reasoning model needs for a normal long answer.

Measured on our instance (SOC triage agents, 4 clients): over the first hour after switching agents from OpenRouter to the direct MiniMax provider, 4 of 56 agent executions (7 %) failed with the error above at 7.3k–11.4k completion tokens; 0 of 209 executions failed that way on OpenRouter the day before. A local patch adding MiniMax to `resolveDefaultMaxOutputTokens` (131072) removed the failures (0 of 21+ executions since).

Suggested fix: give the MiniMax provider a sane default output limit in `resolveDefaultMaxOutputTokens` (e.g. the same 65_536 used for Kimi, or higher), and/or expose `maxOutputTokens` in the Agent `config` so operators can set it per agent. Ideally also surface the AI SDK `compatibility` warning ("The model ... is unknown. The max output tokens have been limited to 4096") in the execution error, so the cause is visible.

### To Reproduce

1. Create a `minimaxApi` credential and an Agent with model `minimax/MiniMax-M3`, `reasoning: high`, no tools needed.
2. Ask it for a long structured answer (e.g. "write a 6000-word incident report with 9 sections").
3. Run it via `Message an Agent` (or the agent chat).
4. The execution fails with "The model reached its output token limit before it returned an answer"; `agent_execution.completionTokens` shows the run stopped around 4k visible output tokens.
5. Same agent with `openrouter/minimax/minimax-m3` completes the same request.

### Expected behavior

The MiniMax provider should not silently cap output at 4096 tokens. Either a realistic default (`resolveDefaultMaxOutputTokens` for `minimax/`) or a configurable `maxOutputTokens` on the Agent, and the underlying "model is unknown, limited to 4096" warning should be visible.

```

Workaround in place: bind-mount over @n8n/agents/dist/runtime/model/provider-quirks.js with

```

### Bug Description

In `packages/core/src/execution-engine/partial-execution-utils/recreate-node-execution-stack.ts`, the `sourceData.complete` and `else` branches disagree about where a connection's data comes from and about what `previousNodeRun` means. The `else` branch (the group that is not complete, i.e. the one that goes to `waitingExecution`) skips pinned data entirely and records the wrong run index.

**1. Pinned data is dropped for an incomplete group.**

`getSourceDataGroups` counts pinned data as data (`get-source-data-groups.ts:98`):

```ts
const hasData = runData[connection.from.name] || pinnedData[connection.from.name];
```

So a group can be marked `complete: false` because of one connection without data, while a *different* connection in the same group has only pinned data.

The complete branch handles that case (`recreate-node-execution-stack.ts:133`):

```ts
if (pinData[sourceNode.name]) {
	incomingData.push(pinData[sourceNode.name]);
} else {
	// ... getIncomingDataFromAnyRun(runData, ...)
}
```

The `else` branch has no such check and only reads `runData` (`:176`):

```ts
const maybeNodeIncomingData = getIncomingDataFromAnyRun(
	runData,
	sourceNode.name,
	incomingConnection.type,
	incomingConnection.outputIndex,
);
const nodeIncomingData = maybeNodeIncomingData?.data ?? null;

if (nodeIncomingData) {
	// added to waitingExecution
}
```

`getIncomingDataFromAnyRun` takes no `pinData` (`get-incoming-data.ts:17`), so for a source that has only pinned data it returns `undefined` and the connection is skipped. The pinned input never reaches `waitingExecution`.

This is reachable, not theoretical: partial execution passes a `runData` that contains *only* the trigger (`packages/cli/src/manual-execution.service.ts:66`):

```ts
const runData = { [data.triggerToStartFrom.name]: [data.triggerToStartFrom.data] };
```

then hands the pinned data in separately as `data.pinData ?? {}` (`:73-78`). So for every source other than the trigger node, pinned data is the *only* source of data, and it is exactly the case the `else` branch does not read.

**2. `previousNodeRun` records the destination's waiting slot, not the source's run.**

In the same block (`:170`):

```ts
const nextRunIndex = waitingExecution[nodeName]
	? Object.keys(waitingExecution[nodeName]).length
	: 0;
```

`nodeName` is the **destination** node, so `nextRunIndex` is the destination's next waiting slot. It is then written as the source's run (`:203`):

```ts
previousNodeRun: nextRunIndex,
```

but `previousNodeRun` describes the node named in `previousNode` (`incomingConnection.from.name`). The complete branch uses the source's run index (`:149` and `:157`):

```ts
runIndex = nodeIncomingData.runIndex;
// ...
previousNodeRun: runIndex,
```

and so does the live engine (`workflow-execute.ts:535-541`), where the value is paired with `parentNodeName`:

```ts
previousNode: parentNodeName,
previousNodeOutput: outputIndex ?? undefined,
previousNodeRun: runIndex ?? undefined,
```

`getIncomingDataFromAnyRun` already returns the source's `runIndex` (`get-incoming-data.ts:29`), so the value is available and unused here.

The existing tests cannot catch this: every `waitingExecutionSource` assertion in `recreate-node-execution-stack.test.ts` has `previousNodeRun: 0`, and `nextRunIndex` is also `0` in those scenarios, so the two agree by coincidence.

**3. Dead branch (minor).**

`:200-206` builds the source with `nodeIncomingData ? { ... } : null`, but the whole block is inside `if (nodeIncomingData)`, so the `: null` arm is unreachable.

### To Reproduce

A unit test against `recreateNodeExecutionStack` reproduces (1). Two inputs on `merge`, input 0 from `node1` with pinned data only, input 1 from `node2` with no data at all:

```ts
const runData: IRunData = {
	[trigger.name]: [toITaskData([{ data: { node: 'trigger' } }])],
};
const pinData: IPinData = {
	[node1.name]: [{ json: { node: 'node1' } }],
};
const startNodes = new Set([merge, node2]);

const { waitingExecution } = recreateNodeExecutionStack(graph, startNodes, runData, pinData);
```

**Actual:** `waitingExecution` has no entry for `merge`, or one without input 0 — the pinned data of `node1` is gone.

**Expected:** `waitingExecution[merge]` contains the pinned data from `node1` for `main[0]`, matching what the `complete` branch does for the same connection.

For (2), the same test with `node1` having run data at run index 1 rather than at 0 shows `previousNodeRun: 0` (the destination slot) where the complete branch and the engine both produce the source's index.

I have not run this against a checkout (I did not install the monorepo here), so please treat the test above as a sketch — it is derived from reading the branches rather than from an executed run.

### Expected behavior

Both branches should agree: a connection in an incomplete group should still contribute pinned data, and `previousNodeRun` should identify the run of the node named in `previousNode`.

### Environment

- n8n version: 2.40.0 (`packages/core/package.json`, `master` at the time of writing)
- Node.js: >= 24 (per `engines` in the root `package.json`)

## Bug Description
The GitLab Trigger's webhook `checkExists` handler reads `error.cause.httpCode` when the GitLab API returns a 404. `gitlabApiRequest` wraps request failures as `NodeApiError`, whose resolved status is available on `error.httpCode`. The fallback then calls `error.description.includes('404')` without checking whether `description` exists. A missing webhook can therefore be handled as an unrelated exception rather than returning `false` and clearing the stale webhook ID; an error without a description can instead throw a `TypeError` while handling the original error.

## To Reproduce
1. Configure a GitLab Trigger with a stored webhook ID.
2. Have its GET `/projects/{project}/hooks/{id}` request reject with a `NodeApiError` whose `httpCode` is `'404'` and whose description is empty or absent.
3. Invoke `webhookMethods.default.checkExists`. The existing `error.cause.httpCode`/`error.description.includes(...)` path does not reliably recognize the 404. The regression tests in PR #35486 exercise this handler directly.

## Expected behavior
A 404 should clear the stale webhook ID/events/secret and return `false` so the webhook can be recreated. Non-404 errors should propagate unchanged, including errors without a description.

This report is for the error-handling branch of `checkExists`, not the unrelated DELETE failure discussed in #4217. Fix and regression tests: #35486.

title: Postgres node: a comma in a query-parameter value is split into several bind values

judge.reasoning:
Both patches attack the same root cause: in the nodeVersion >= 2.5 branch, an evaluated expression result is run through isJSON()/stringToArray() and split on commas. Patch A replaces that with a single `values.push(evaluateExpression(rawEvaluated))`, which is exactly the fix the issue proposes, and leaves the literal-only branch's stringToArray split intact for backward compatibility. It applies to every affected version (2.5 through 2.7), so the reporter's existing webhook-ingestion workflow at typeVersion 2.5 is fixed without the user rebuilding the node. This matches the precedent already visible in the same block: the adjacent array-spread fix (#31704) sits inside the >= 2.5 branch with no further version gate. A's tests are targeted and would fail on base: the comma, multi-comma, three-parameter, empty-string and numeric cases all assert the exact bind-value array passed to runQueries, plus a regression test that literal comma lists still split. The edits to the two existing tests are a necessary consequence of removing isJSON from the operation (the old 'invalid JSON' test asserted the buggy split).

Patch B implements the same one-value-per-expression rule but only for a new node version 2.8, leaving 2.5–2.7 deliberately broken; its own test 'split a value that contains a comma before v2.8' locks in the bug for every existing workflow, which is the configuration the issue reports. Version gating is a legitimate n8n convention and does protect anyone relying on `.join(',')` in an expression, but B goes well beyond the ask: it changes array undefined-elements to SQL NULL, converts the single-expression null/undefined path from a thrown NodeOperationError to `[null]`, maps null/undefined expression results to NULL, duplicates the entire Query Parameters option with version-conditioned displayOptions, and adds a descriptions test. None of this is requested, each piece is a separate behaviour change, and together they obscure the two-line fix and widen the risk surface. B's tests are thorough but a large share verify the unrelated null handling.

The independent tests crashed on all three trees (collection failure, exit 9), so they provide no discriminating evidence. Weighing correctness first, A resolves the reported issue for the versions the issue names with a minimal, well-tested change; B resolves it only for a version that does not yet exist in users' workflows and bundles unrelated semantics changes. A wins, with the caveat that an ungated change could affect anyone who intentionally joined values with commas inside an expression.

issue_md:
> **⚠️ Severity corrected after further testing.** An earlier version of this report
> claimed *silent data corruption*. That was wrong: I had verified n8n's value
> **collection** but not the value **binding**. Supplying the surplus value to
> PostgreSQL produces a hard error, not a wrong write. See the
> [correction comment](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/issues/40022#issuecomment-5919564259).
> The code path and the fix suggestion are unchanged.

**Affected version:** 2.41.3 — and current `master`. The code is byte-identical in both
(verified against `n8n@2.41.3` and `master`: same statements, same line numbers).
**Node version:** `typeVersion` 2.5 and above, i.e. the current branch.
**Impact:** the query fails with a parameter-count error that does not point at the real
cause. No incorrect data is written.

## Summary

The Postgres node tells users to use `$1, $2, …` with **Query Parameters** to avoid SQL
injection. When a parameter's evaluated value is a **string containing a comma that is not
itself valid JSON**, the node splits that one value into several bind values. The
resulting parameter count no longer matches the statement, and execution fails with an
error that blames the *count* rather than the comma in the user's data.

## Affected code

`packages/nodes-base/nodes/Postgres/v2/actions/database/executeQuery.operation.ts`,
inside the `nodeVersion >= 2.5` branch (lines 106–108 in both 2.41.3 and `master`):

```ts
const evaluatedExpression = evaluateExpression(rawEvaluated);
const evaluatedValues = isJSON(evaluatedExpression)
    ? [evaluatedExpression]
    : stringToArray(evaluatedExpression);

if (evaluatedValues.length) values.push(...evaluatedValues);
```

`stringToArray` (`helpers/utils.ts`) is a comma split with empty filtering and trimming:

```ts
export function stringToArray(str: NodeParameterValueType | undefined) {
	if (str === undefined) return [];
	return String(str)
		.split(',')
		.filter((entry) => entry)
		.map((entry) => entry.trim());
}
```

So a single parameter whose evaluated value is `O'Brien, Test` contributes **two** bind
values instead of one.

## Why `isJSON()` does not save you

`evaluateExpression` (`helpers/utils.ts`) returns plain strings via `toString()` — it does
**not** JSON-encode them:

```ts
return typeof expression === 'object' ? JSON.stringify(expression) : expression.toString();
```

So `isJSON()` returns `true` only when the *data itself* happens to parse as JSON:

| evaluated value | `isJSON` | bind values produced | correct? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `123` | true | 1 | yes |
| `true` | true | 1 | yes |
| `Doe, John` | **false** | **2** | **no** |
| `O'Brien, Test` | **false** | **2** | **no** |
| `hello, world, again` | **false** | **3** | **no** |

This is why casual testing tends to pass: a numeric or boolean-looking value behaves
correctly, while ordinary free text does not. It is **data-dependent**, which is the most
dangerous shape for a bug in a form/webhook ingestion path.

## Reproduction

1. Add a **Postgres** node, operation **Execute Query**, with **Query Parameters** on.
2. Query: `SELECT $1::text AS a, $2::text AS b` — two placeholders.
3. Query parameters, in the node's `options.queryReplacement`:
   - `={{ $json.name }}`
   - `={{ $json.note }}`
4. Feed webhook/Code-node data: `{ "name": "Doe, John", "note": "hello" }`
5. Execute.

### Verified — value collection, using the node's own logic

`isJSON`, `evaluateExpression` and `stringToArray` copied verbatim from `helpers/utils.ts`,
plus the `nodeVersion >= 2.5` branch copied verbatim, mocking only `getResolvables()` and
the expression evaluator. Observed bind values:

```
no commas   {name:"Smith",      note:"hello"}                 -> ["Smith","hello"]           correct
comma in $1 {name:"Doe, John", note:"hello"}                 -> ["Doe","John","hello"]       3 values, 2 placeholders
3 params    {name:"Doe, John", note:"hello", city:"Galena"}   -> ["Doe","John","hello","Galena"]  4 values, 3
legacy <2.5 {name:"Doe, John", note:"hello"}                 -> ["Doe, John","hello"]         SAFE
array       {tags:["a","b","c"]}                             -> ["a","b","c"]                 #31704 fix present
```

### Verified — what the database then does

```
BEGIN;
CREATE TEMP TABLE reprobind (a text, b text);
PREPARE two (text, text) AS INSERT INTO reprobind VALUES ($1, $2) RETURNING a, b;
EXECUTE two('Doe', 'John', 'hello');
```
```
ERROR:  wrong number of parameters for prepared statement "two"
DETAIL:  Expected 2 parameters but got 3.
```

The driver rejects the surplus value; it does not drop it and does not shift the remaining
bindings.

**This can never be silent.** `stringToArray` splits on commas and filters empties, so a
value containing a comma can only ever *add* to the parameter count, never reduce it.
`values.length` is therefore always `>=` the number of expressions supplied, so the count
either overshoots the placeholders (*"Expected N but got M"*) or undershoots them (the
mirror error). It can never accidentally re-align.

## Note on the `nodeVersion < 2.5` branch

The older branch splits the **raw** parameter string (`rawReplacements.replace(/^=+/, '').split(',')`)
and then pushes each *evaluated* result **whole**:

```ts
for (const rawValue of rawValues) {
    const resolvables = getResolvables(rawValue);
    if (resolvables.length) {
        for (const resolvable of resolvables) {
            values.push(this.evaluateExpression(`${resolvable}`, index) as IDataObject);
        }
    } else {
        values.push(rawValue);
    }
}
```

Because the split is applied *before* evaluation, commas inside the **data** are safe
there. The hazard is in the newer branch, where the split is applied *after* evaluation.

## Relationship to #30978 / #31704

#30978 reported that a JS **array** was wrapped as a single bind value because of the same
`isJSON()` mismatch, and #31704 (merged 2026-06-04) fixed it by spreading arrays. That fix
handles `Array.isArray(rawEvaluated)` and does not change the `isJSON() ? … : stringToArray(…)`
path for **strings**, so the comma case described here remains. This looks like the
remaining half of the same underlying problem: the node cannot reliably distinguish "a
string that is one value" from "a comma-separated list of values".

## Suggested fix

Keep the ability to pass several literal parameters, but never split a value that came
from an expression. Concretely, in the `nodeVersion >= 2.5` branch, when the raw parameter
contained a resolvable, push the evaluated result as exactly one value, and reserve
`stringToArray` for parameters that are literal text with no `{{ }}`:

```ts
if (resolvables.length) {
    for (const resolvable of resolvables) {
        const rawEvaluated = this.evaluateExpression(`${resolvable}`, index);
        if (Array.isArray(rawEvaluated)) {
            for (const item of rawEvaluated) { /* unchanged */ }
            continue;
        }
        // an expression evaluates to exactly one value
        values.push(evaluateExpression(rawEvaluated));
    }
} else {
    values.push(...stringToArray(rawValues));
}
```

If comma-splitting of *literal* parameters must be preserved for backwards compatibility,
that is the branch to keep it in. The current behaviour appears to be unintentional: a
single expression is expected to yield a single bind value everywhere else in the node.

Happy to open a PR with tests if that is useful.

## Environment

- n8n 2.41.3, self-hosted
- Postgres node `typeVersion` 2.5
- Observed on a form/webhook ingestion workflow storing free-text customer input

## Bug description

After upgrading two self-hosted Postgres-backed instances from 2.32.7 to 2.42.6, the main process log fills with the same error every ~20-30 seconds, indefinitely:

```
value too long for type character varying(36)
QueryFailedError: value too long for type character varying(36)
    at PostgresQueryRunner.query (.../@n8n/typeorm/driver/postgres/PostgresQueryRunner.js:218:19)
    at InsertQueryBuilder.execute (.../@n8n/typeorm/query-builder/InsertQueryBuilder.js:95:33)
    at .../@n8n/db/src/repositories/workflow-publication-trigger-status.repository.ts:43:4
    at WorkflowPublicationTriggerStatusRepository.replaceForWorkflow (...:40:3)
    at .../src/workflows/publication/publication-status-reporter.ts:281:5
    at process (.../src/workflows/publication/workflow-publication-outbox-consumer.ts:392:7)
    at WorkflowPublicationLifecycleLock.runExclusive (.../workflow-publication-lifecycle-lock.ts:47:11)
```

Cause: the new `workflow_publication_trigger_status` table (created by the 2.42 migrations) defines `nodeId` as `character varying(36)`:

```
workflowId  character varying(36)
nodeId      character varying(36)
versionId   character varying(36)
status      character varying(20)
...
```

However, node ids are not guaranteed to be 36-char UUIDs. Workflows created or imported through the API/JSON import can carry arbitrary user-assigned node id strings, and n8n has accepted those for years. On our instances several long-standing active workflows have descriptive node ids such as `telegram-fallback-HetrixTools-Notification` (38 chars, `n8n-nodes-base.telegram` nodes).

When the publication status reporter tries to record trigger status for such a workflow, the INSERT in `replaceForWorkflow` fails, and the publication outbox consumer retries the same failing insert forever, producing continuous log noise (~2-3 errors/min per affected workflow set).

## To reproduce

1. On a Postgres-backed 2.42.x instance, import a workflow whose JSON gives a node an `id` longer than 36 characters (e.g. `"id": "telegram-fallback-my-descriptive-node-name"`), with any trigger node so it can be activated.
2. Activate the workflow.
3. Watch the main process log: `QueryFailedError: value too long for type character varying(36)` from `WorkflowPublicationTriggerStatusRepository.replaceForWorkflow`, retried indefinitely by `workflow-publication-outbox-consumer`.

Instances where every node id is a 36-char UUID show zero occurrences.

## Expected behavior

Either the schema accepts the ids that n8n itself accepts elsewhere (widen `nodeId`, e.g. `varchar(128)` or `text`), or the reporter skips/truncates oversized ids. In any case the outbox consumer should not retry a deterministic constraint failure forever.

## Impact

Executions, triggers and the editor are unaffected (verified: the affected workflows keep executing successfully). The impact is unbounded log noise and the publication trigger status never being recorded for those workflows.

## Environment

- n8n 2.42.6, official Docker image (`docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:2.42.6`), upgraded from 2.32.7
- Reproduced on two independent instances: PostgreSQL 17 (`pgvector/pgvector:pg17`) and PostgreSQL 15 (`postgres:15`)
- Regular mode (no queue) on both affected instances
- OS: Ubuntu 24.04 hosts, docker compose deployments

+/**

+ * `varchar(255)`. Node ids are UUIDs only when the editor generates them:
+ * workflows created through the API or JSON import carry arbitrary strings

+

+			await runQuery(
+				`ALTER TABLE ${escape.tableName(table)} ALTER COLUMN ${escape.columnName(column)} TYPE VARCHAR(${NODE_ID_LENGTH})`,
+			);
+		}
+	}

### Bug Description

In a production queue-mode deployment, we observed waiting sub-workflow entries accumulating in a worker’s `ActiveExecutions` registry. Sampled execution IDs had already completed successfully, but their original in-memory entries remained.

Two production samples taken approximately 73 minutes apart showed:
- Waiting entries increased from 6,439 to 9,776.
- All entries from the earlier sample were still present in the later sample.
- Sampled executions corresponding to retained entries had already completed successfully.

These observations show retained entries in the sampled worker. They do not establish the status of every retained execution, quantify the associated memory usage, or prove that this causes an out-of-memory crash.

Suspected cause:
Integrated sub-workflows initially execute in their parent worker. When they enter a persisted wait, their execution data can remain in that worker’s `ActiveExecutions`. They subsequently resume as queue jobs, whose completion does not appear to remove the original entries.

Related proposed fix: https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/pull/39224

The PR reports seven added regression tests, all 196 relevant tests passing, and CLI lint and type checking passing. Restoring the old cleanup logic caused two regression tests to fail as expected.

Limitations:
- The issue has not yet been reproduced in an unmodified upstream deployment.
- Queue-mode integration validation of the proposed fix has not been completed.
- Before-and-after memory measurements and validation against the latest upstream code are still needed.

### To Reproduce

A verified minimal reproduction is not yet available. The issue was observed through production worker inspection.

title: Instance AI / Agents: thread keeps using a deleted sandbox after the runner restarts ("sandbox not found") and never recreates it

judge.reasoning:
Both patches implement the core ask: wrap remote sandbox calls (exec and filesystem ops) so a `404 sandbox not found` drops the cached running state via markNeedsStart, re-POSTs /sandboxes with the deterministic id through ensureRunning, and retries the op exactly once. Neither independent test run produced results on any tree, so the verdict rests on the diffs.

Patch A detects the condition by regex-matching the error message (`/sandbox not found/i`) and also adjusts `exists()` so a missing sandbox is not reported as a missing file. It wraps getInfo as well. Tests are focused and cover recovery, retry-once, non-matching 404s, getInfo and exists. Weaknesses: detection is coupled to the service's message text, and concurrent failures each trigger their own recreate (harmless since POST with the same id is idempotent, but unguarded).

Patch B detects by probing `GET /sandboxes/{id}` on any 404 (bounded by a 10s timeout) and only recreates when the probe itself 404s, which is independent of message wording and still distinguishes file-not-found from sandbox-not-found. It dedupes concurrent recoveries with a shared promise and tests that explicitly. Crucially, B also addresses the second half of the issue's expectation ("the thread keeps working"): after recreation the sandbox is empty, but the cached RuntimeSandboxEntry still has setupComplete=true, so setupSandboxWorkspace (templates, skills, knowledge base) would never re-run until n8n restarts, leaving the agent on a bare sandbox. B checks the `.sandbox-initialized` marker for the n8n-sandbox provider and re-runs setup when it is gone, with tests at the service layer. That is extra scope, but it is directly needed for the recovered thread to actually function, not unrelated churn. Costs: an extra marker read per message for the n8n-sandbox provider, an extra probe roundtrip on ordinary file-not-found 404s, getInfo is left unwrapped, and the probe passes a promise (not a thunk) to raceWithAbort, which I cannot verify from the diff but is consistent with the existing `creation` promise pattern in createSandbox.

On correctness B is more robust in detection and more complete in restoring a working thread; on tests both are substantive, B slightly broader (concurrency, probe timeout, service-layer re-setup). A is cleaner and smaller, but B's advantages outweigh its added complexity.

### Bug Description

With the `n8n-sandbox` provider, an existing Agent / n8n Assistant thread stays broken after its remote sandbox disappears (for example after the sandbox runner restarts). n8n keeps calling `POST /sandboxes/{id}/executions` for the thread's deterministic sandbox id, gets `404 sandbox not found` every time, and never calls `POST /sandboxes` to recreate it. The agent replies that the sandbox is unreachable and gives up. New threads work fine.

This persists even after n8n itself has restarted, so it is not only the in-process sandbox cache: on a cache miss n8n reuses the id directly instead of re-creating the sandbox.

The sandbox service already supports the recovery path. `docs/API.md` in `n8n-io/n8n-sandbox-service` says a runner restart makes a sandbox return 404, and that `POST /sandboxes` with a caller-supplied `id` returns the existing sandbox or recreates it with the same id. Calling `POST /sandboxes {"id": "<thread sandbox id>"}` by hand fixed the broken thread immediately.

Timeline from the `sandbox-api` logs (UTC, one thread):

- 20:15:16 `POST /sandboxes` 201, sandbox `df02d17e-...` created for the thread, then executions 200
- 20:40:33 Docker Engine upgrade restarts all containers (sandbox-api, runner, n8n); n8n back at 20:40:45
- 20:44:35 to 21:13:51 `POST /sandboxes/df02d17e-.../executions` 404, 26 times, no `POST /sandboxes` for that id in between
- 21:15 manual `POST /sandboxes {"id":"df02d17e-..."}` 201, the thread works again

```
{"level":"INFO","msg":"request","method":"POST","path":"/sandboxes/df02d17e-08d3-5cb7-900b-7d53f03c4cc4/executions","query":"","status":404,"duration_ms":0}
```

### To Reproduce

1. Self-hosted n8n with the `n8n-sandbox` provider (services as in `docker/get-n8n-compose.yml`), connected from Settings > Agents > Shared sandbox.
2. Open an Agent builder or n8n Assistant thread and send a message that uses the workspace, so the thread's sandbox is created.
3. Restart the sandbox runner. In our case this happened through a Docker Engine upgrade, which restarted every container including n8n. Restarting only the runner (`docker compose restart sandbox-runner-1`) should be enough according to the API docs, but we did not test that variant.
4. Send another message in the same thread.

The sandbox-api logs show only 404s on `/sandboxes/{id}/executions` for the thread's id, and the agent reports "sandbox not found".

### Expected behavior

When the sandbox service answers `404 sandbox not found`, n8n should drop the cached entry, call `POST /sandboxes` with the thread's deterministic id (which returns the existing sandbox or recreates it), and retry the request once, as the API docs already recommend for `409 sandbox_restarted`. Workspace files are lost, but the thread keeps working.

Workaround we use for now: a cron job on the host that records the ids from `GET /sandboxes` every minute and re-POSTs them when the runner's start time changes.

judge.reasoning: Both patches make the core layout change the issue proposes (`flex: 1 0 auto` with the existing `min-width` floor), which lets the card grow and the strip scroll instead of painting over the neighbour. Patch A stops there: it adds no `min-width: 0`/nowrap guards on `.valueRow`, `.value`, or the delta badge, does not touch the 6-decimal `formatMetricNumber` that the issue identifies as the reason both strings are wide, leaves the unscaled custom metric with no value tooltip, and includes an unrelated `as-child` change to the title tooltip. With flex-basis auto and no handling of `.titleRow`, a long metric name would now widen the card instead of ellipsizing as it did under the fixed track, a side effect A does not address. Patch A adds no tests. Patch B implements both halves of the suggested fix: the same flex change, `min-width: 0` on `.valueRow` as the guard, `white-space: nowrap`/`flex-shrink: 0` on the value and badge so they can never wrap or be squeezed, a `.titleRow` width trick so long names still ellipsize rather than drive card width, a ~4-significant-digit cap in `formatMetricNumber` (with sensible handling for >=1000 and float noise), and a new `formatMetricExactValue` that populates the previously empty tooltip with the full-precision value (also applied consistently to `TestCaseMetricRow`, which shares the helper). B adds unit tests for the compact/exact formatting and component tests asserting the compact rendering and the hover tooltip, which would fail on base. The independent test crashed on all three trees, so it provides no signal. issue_md: ## Describe the bug #40852 fixed the formatting half of #40844 — custom `setMetrics` values are no longer squashed into percentages, and that part works exactly as hoped. But raw values are much wider than the `73%` strings the summary strip was laid out for, and the card cannot grow or clip, so the value and its delta badge paint on top of the neighbouring card. In the screenshot (Run #39, 17 custom metrics): `Jev Legible Confidence`'s value `0.7` and its `-0.037` badge are drawn on top of `Jev Legible Norm`'s `+0.084333` badge, and the same happens between `Jev Faithful` and `Judge Match Ok`, whose value `1` is buried under the badge to its left. ## Why it happens `MetricSummaryCard.vue` gives each card a fixed track that cannot shrink and does not clip: ```scss flex: 1 0 calc(var(--spacing--4xl) + var(--spacing--3xl)); /* 128px + 64px = 192px */ padding: var(--spacing--md) var(--spacing--lg); /* 24px each side */ ``` That leaves **144px** of content box. `.valueRow` is `display: flex` with `flex-wrap: nowrap`, no `min-width: 0` and no `overflow`, holding: - the value at `--font-size--2xl` (28px) — `0.728333` is roughly 120px of glyphs, - `--spacing--sm` (16px) of gap, - the `TrendDeltaBadge`, itself an icon plus `+0.084333` at `--font-size--sm`, roughly another 100px. So ~240px of content in a 144px box, with `flex-shrink: 0` and `overflow: visible` — the surplus is painted over whatever sits to the right. Both strings come from the same helper added in #40852, which is why the value *and* the delta are wide: ```ts function formatMetricNumber(value: number): string { return value.toLocaleString(undefined, { maximumFractionDigits: 6 }); } ``` This only shows up for unscaled custom metrics, because `formatMetricPercent` keeps every other category to 3–4 characters. ## To Reproduce 1. On a workflow with evaluations, emit two or more custom metrics whose values are not round — e.g. `0.728333`, `0.833333`, `0.777778` (an average over 14 rows produces these naturally). 2. Run the evaluation twice, so the cards also render a delta badge. 3. Open the run detail. Adjacent cards overlap; the narrower the viewport and the more metrics, the more of them collide. ## Expected behaviour A metric card is at least as wide as the value and delta it renders, and never draws over the card next to it. ## Suggested fix Two small changes, in the spirit of #40852: **1. Let the card size to its content** — `MetricSummaryStrip.vue` already wraps the row in an `ElScrollbar`, so a wider row scrolls instead of colliding: ```diff - flex: 1 0 calc(var(--spacing--4xl) + var(--spacing--3xl)); + flex: 1 0 auto; min-width: calc(var(--spacing--4xl) + var(--spacing--3xl)); ``` `min-width` keeps today's floor for short values, `flex-grow: 1` still fills the strip when there are only a few metrics. **2. Keep the tile readable** — six decimals is more than a summary tile needs, and the delta needs it even less. Capping `formatMetricNumber` to about four significant digits (`0.7283`, `1`, `0.8333`) keeps the cards compact while the exact value stays available on hover. Note that unscaled custom metrics currently have **no** value tooltip at all: `formattedSumScore` is `''` for them, so `valueTooltip` is empty — worth populating it with the full-precision value as part of this. Optionally `min-width: 0` on `.valueRow` as a guard, so no future change to either string can paint over a neighbour again. Both are covered by the test files #40852 added (`evaluation.utils.test.ts`, `MetricSummaryStrip.test.ts`). Happy to open a PR for this if that helps. ## Environment - n8n version: 2.45.4 (self-hosted, Docker, SQLite) - First affected release: 2.45.0, where #40852 shipped - Browser: Chrome

issue_md:
### Bug Description

When n8n uses PostgreSQL and the PostgreSQL session time zone is not UTC (e.g. the server's `timezone` setting is a local zone, which is the Debian `initdb` default), the `startedAfter` / `startedBefore` filters of the executions list are applied shifted by the zone's UTC offset. With a UTC+2 server time zone, both bounds act 2 hours earlier than requested.

Affected: the instance-level MCP tool `search_workflow_executions` and the date filter of the executions list (same query path). The stored `startedAt` values and the values returned in responses are correct; only the filter is shifted.

**Root cause (from the source of `n8n@2.47.7`):**

1. `packages/@n8n/db/src/repositories/execution.repository.ts`, `startedAtCondition()`:
   `MoreThanOrEqual(DateUtils.mixedDateToUtcDatetimeString(new Date(startedAfter)))` (same for `startedBefore`).
2. `DateUtils.mixedDateToUtcDatetimeString` (`@n8n/typeorm`) builds `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss.SSS` from `getUTC*()` — a UTC wall-clock string **without a zone designator**.
3. On Postgres, `execution_entity."startedAt"` is `timestamptz` (`datetimeColumnType`).
4. Postgres interprets a zone-less literal compared against `timestamptz` in the **session** `TimeZone`. n8n does not set the session time zone in its connection options, so the server default applies.

So `08:20:00` (meant as UTC) is read as `08:20:00+02` = `06:20:00Z`.

The same pattern is used in `getIdsSince()` and `getWorkflowIdsWithExecutionsSince()`. The `waitTill` queries only use it for SQLite and pass `Date` objects on Postgres, so they are not affected.

Related: #25054 (same helper, write path of `startedAt`, also non-UTC Postgres) was closed without merge; the write path is correct in 2.47.7, the filter path is not.

### To Reproduce

1. Run n8n with `DB_TYPE=postgresdb` against a Postgres whose `timezone` is a non-UTC zone with a positive offset (e.g. `ALTER DATABASE n8n SET timezone = 'Etc/GMT-2'`, i.e. UTC+2), restart n8n.
2. Have an execution with `startedAt = 2026-11-14T06:20:30Z`.
3. Call `search_workflow_executions` with `startedAfter=2026-11-14T06:20:00Z`, `startedBefore=2026-11-14T06:21:00Z` → empty result.
4. Call it with `startedAfter=2026-11-14T08:20:00Z`, `startedBefore=2026-11-14T08:21:00Z` → the 06:20:30Z execution is returned.
5. Set the session zone to UTC for the n8n role (`ALTER ROLE n8n IN DATABASE n8n SET timezone = 'UTC'`), restart n8n → step 3 returns the execution, step 4 is empty.

### Expected behavior

The filter bounds are compared as absolute instants, independent of the Postgres session time zone — e.g. pass `Date` objects (or ISO strings with an offset) for Postgres instead of zone-less UTC strings, or set the session time zone to UTC in the Postgres connection options.

### Debug Info

Self-hosted, official Docker image `n8nio/n8n:2.47.7`, container `TZ=UTC`, `GENERIC_TIMEZONE` set to a UTC+2 zone (not relevant to the bug; the shift follows the Postgres session time zone). External PostgreSQL 17 with server `timezone` UTC+2. Workaround applied: role-level `timezone = 'UTC'`.

Debian 13 (Docker)

### n8n Version

2.47.7

### Node.js Version

bundled with the official Docker image 2.47.7

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Execution mode

main (default)

self hosted

title: Microsoft Outlook v1 Add attachment reads the binary field name from item 0 for every item

judge.reasoning: The source change is byte-identical in both patches: the single-line switch from index 0 to index i in the v1 messageAttachment add loop, which is exactly the root cause the issue names. So correctness and scope are tied, and the decision rests on the tests. Both tests exercise the issue's scenario (two items, binary fields 'data' and 'attachment', per-item binaryPropertyName) and both would fail on base because the second item would look up 'data', which is absent, and throw. Both assert getBinaryDataBuffer is called with (0,'data') and (1,'attachment'), which is the direct observable of the fix. The difference is Patch A's extra assertions. A mocks getBinaryDataBuffer to resolve Buffer.from('content') and then asserts the request body contains contentBytes 'c2Vjb25k', the raw base64 of the second item's binary data. Those two choices are mutually inconsistent: the node calls getBinaryDataBuffer precisely to build contentBytes from the buffer (the call would be pointless otherwise), so with that mock the real contentBytes would be the base64 of 'content', not 'c2Vjb25k', and A's test would most likely fail even with the fix applied. A also relies on a pass-through returnJsonArray mock and an exact result shape of [[{success:true},{success:true}]], which couples the test to downstream helpers that are not what the issue is about. Patch B keeps its assertions to what the issue specifies: execution completes, getBinaryDataBuffer is called exactly twice, and each call uses the current item's field name. That test is internally consistent and has no assertion that contradicts its own mocks. The independent harness runs crashed on all three trees, so they provide no signal either way. Given identical fixes, B wins on test craft: a focused test that is very likely to pass after the fix beats a broader test that probably fails because of a self-contradictory mock.
